analysis.one_liner: Taxes newly made plastic used in single-use products to fund recycling and ocean cleanup.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to four House committees and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The REDUCE Act would charge plastics manufacturers and importers a tax of 10 to 20 cents per pound on newly made (virgin) plastic resin, with the rate rising over time and adjusted for inflation. Plastic used in single-use products like packaging, beverage containers, food service items, and bags would be taxed; recycled resin would be exempt, and makers of medical products, drug containers, and hygiene products would be excluded. The money would go into a Plastic Waste Reduction Fund for recycling infrastructure, marine debris cleanup, and addressing pollution impacts on communities near plastics production. The bill never advanced past committee referrals.
analysis.who_benefits: Coastal and waterfront communities affected by plastic waste and marine debris, communities living near plastics production facilities, and the recycling industry, which would gain demand for recycled resin that the bill exempts from the tax.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Coastal communities, recyclers, and fenceline neighborhoods

how_it_helps.text: Creates a dedicated Plastic Waste Reduction Fund, funded entirely by the plastics tax, to pay for recycling infrastructure improvements, marine debris detection, monitoring, and cleanup under existing federal programs, and to address environmental justice and pollution impacts from plastic production [S3].

Gives recycled plastic a price advantage: post-consumer recycled resin is expressly excluded from the tax, while newly made virgin resin is taxed at 10 cents per pound in 2022, 15 cents in 2023, and 20 cents in 2024, rising with inflation thereafter [S3].

Places the tax at the source on manufacturers, producers, and importers of more than 10 tons of virgin resin per year, and taxes imported single-use plastic items equally so domestic producers are not disadvantaged against imports [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Petrochemical and plastics manufacturers, who pay the per-pound tax on virgin resin, and to the extent they pass costs along, buyers of single-use plastic packaging, bottles, and food service items. Producers of non-covered products can claim a refund of tax paid on resin used in them [S3].

drawbacks.text: The tax would raise the cost of single-use plastic products, which are used heavily in food and beverages, and some of that cost would likely reach consumers, including lower-income households [S3].

The revenue depends on continued plastic production; if producers successfully shift to recycled resin, fund receipts would shrink, so cleanup and recycling programs would be funded by the very activity being discouraged [S3].
A per-pound tax does not by itself guarantee that plastic waste declines; it depends on how much manufacturers actually substitute recycled or non-plastic materials in response [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a modest, well-aimed tax: it targets the least-recycled plastic (virgin resin going into single-use items), exempts recycled resin and medically necessary plastic, refunds the tax for non-single-use products, and directs the revenue to cleanup and recycling rather than general spending. The main honest cost is some price pass-through on everyday packaged goods. Its main design weakness is that its funding source shrinks if it succeeds at discouraging virgin plastic.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to four House committees on the day it was introduced, then to two subcommittees two days later, and no hearing, markup, or vote ever happened before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Thomas Suozzi introduced the bill on September 27, 2021, and it was referred that day to the Ways and Means, Energy and Commerce, Natural Resources, and Transportation and Infrastructure Committees [S1][S5].

On September 28, 2021, it was referred to the Coast Guard and Maritime Transportation Subcommittee and the Environment and Climate Change Subcommittee; no further action of any kind appears in the record for the rest of the 117th Congress [S5].
Six House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republican cosponsor joined [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Virgin plastics and petrochemical producers avoided a new per-pound tax, and makers of single-use plastic packaging faced no new cost; no new money flowed to recycling or marine debris cleanup.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Virgin plastics producers, which avoided the tax

against.name: Richard E. Neal
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee (primary tax-writing committee)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or other consideration of the bill after it was referred to the committee; the record shows no action beyond the referral for the rest of the Congress [S5].

sides.party_line_note: All seven sponsors were Democrats and no Republican cosponsored, but there was no hearing or vote, so no recorded opposition or split exists to measure.

industries.note: The bill taxes their core product, virgin resin, at 10-20 cents per pound for resin going into single-use items, with the rate rising over time. The industry's interest in blocking the bill ran against the public's interest in funding cleanup and reducing plastic waste.

industries.industry: Consumer packaged goods and food/beverage companies that use single-use plastic packaging
industries.note: Importers of covered items and producers using taxed resin would face the tax and some price increases, but they could claim refunds for resin used in non-covered products and could avoid the tax by using recycled resin. Their lower costs came at the price of no new cleanup funding.
Post-consumer recycled resin is exempt from the tax, giving recyclers a price advantage over virgin plastic, and the fund would pay for recycling infrastructure improvements.

industries.industry: Medical products and pharmaceutical packaging makers
industries.note: Their products are exempted from the covered-item tax on public health and safety grounds, but resin taxed on entry could still raise input costs; the narrow exemption protects most of their market.
